This is the deliberately pedestrian companion to the library module: it uses the same tested functions, but shows every pricing decision instead of hiding it in `main()`. The full freMTPL2 run can take a while; use a small sample only to check that the notebook works, not to draw actuarial conclusions. That pairing — *the idea in a few lines, the tested version underneath* — is what the chapter is for. ::: {#27d39e84 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from inspect import getsource from itertools import combinations import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from IPython.display import Markdown, display from nonlife_pureprem import ( TARGET_SPECS, coefficient_relativity_table, evaluate_predictions, exposure_balanced_double_lift_table, exposure_balanced_lift_table, fit_glum_inference, fit_glum_predictive, fit_lightgbm, gini, grouped_calibration, lift_diagnostics, lightgbm_frame, load_mtpl2, lorenz_curve, lorenz_dominance_table, make_splits, portfolio_calibration_table, print_frame, select_tweedie_power, target_and_weight, target_weight_table, weighted_mean_deviance, ) def show_source(fn): """Render a library function as a syntax-highlighted code block.""" display(Markdown(f"```python\n{getsource(fn)}\n```")) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A note on figures All charts in this chapter are produced by inline matplotlib cells — they render as native cell outputs, and the plotting code is right there to read. The library's `save_core_figures` helper is used by the CLI to write the same four figures to disk; it is intentionally not used here. ::: ## Set a reproducible run **Why:** a comparison is only credible when every model sees the same data split and tuning budget. **What we do:** keep the production defaults below. Set `n_samples` only for a quick software smoke run. **Best practice:** fix the random seed and comparison protocol before looking at results. Do not use a convenience sample to select a rate model. ::: {#f86b0c56 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_samples = None # e.g. 10_000 for a quick software smoke run n_alphas = 30 max_rounds = 2_000 early_stopping_rounds = 50 ``` ::: ## Build audited frequency, severity, and pure-premium targets **Why:** a model cannot repair an incoherent target. Frequency, severity, and pure premium each represent a rate over a different amount of risk. **What we do:** load policy and claim tables, remove non-positive claims, cap each claim, aggregate claims to policy level, and construct the three targets. **Best practice:** reconcile source claim counts with claim records, choose and document the cap before fitting, and use exposure for frequency and pure premium but claim count for claim-weighted severity. ::: {#61fe64dd .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} data, audit = load_mtpl2(n_samples=n_samples) print_frame("Target and weight definitions", target_weight_table()) print_frame("Claim preparation", pd.DataFrame([audit])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Portfolio averages by hand The portfolio averages are the exposure-weighted means of the rates. Because frequency, severity, and pure premium are each a risk-volume rate, the weighted mean of the rate equals the unweighted ratio of the underlying claim amounts: ::: {#ff368c18 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} avg_frequency = data["ClaimNb"].sum() / data["Exposure"].sum() avg_frequency_check = np.average(data["Frequency"], weights=data["Exposure"]) avg_pure_premium = data["ClaimAmountCapped"].sum() / data["Exposure"].sum() avg_pure_premium_check = np.average(data["PurePremium"], weights=data["Exposure"]) print(f"Average frequency: {avg_frequency:.6f} claim / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_frequency_check:.6f}") print(f"Average pure premium: {avg_pure_premium:.2f} EUR / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_pure_premium_check:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average frequency: 0.073792 claim / year check (weighted mean of rate): 0.073792 Average pure premium: 137.58 EUR / year check (weighted mean of rate): 137.58 ``` ::: ::: The two ways of writing the average are identical because each rate is defined as `amount / volume`. The same identity is what makes the target × weight multiplication collapse to the underlying claim amounts in `portfolio_calibration_table` and `evaluate_predictions`. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `TARGET_SPECS` and `target_and_weight` The whole frequency / severity / pure-premium weighting decision lives in `TARGET_SPECS` and the `target_and_weight` helper that unpacks it. ::: {#9700d439 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(target_and_weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def target_and_weight( data: pd.DataFrame, component: str, ) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """Return the rows, target, and weights for one pricing component.""" spec = TARGET_SPECS[component] rows = data.loc[data["ClaimNb"] > 0] if spec.claims_only else data return ( rows, rows[spec.target].to_numpy(dtype=float), rows[spec.weight].to_numpy(dtype=float), ) ``` ::: ::: Key points: - `frequency` uses target `Frequency` with weight `Exposure` over all policies. - `severity` uses target `Severity` with weight `ClaimNb` over **claims only** — the `claims_only` flag filters rows to `ClaimNb > 0` so the average is the claim-amount weighted mean of the conditional severity. - `pure_premium` uses target `PurePremium` with weight `Exposure` over all policies. Multiplying by exposure recovers the total capped claim amount. ::: ## Reserve a test set before making modelling choices **Why:** test performance is evidence only when test policies did not influence feature choices, Tweedie power, or LightGBM tuning. **What we do:** make a fixed train/test split, then split training data into development-train and development-validation data. **Best practice:** tune on development validation, refit once on all training data, and inspect the untouched test set last. Also repeat by time or geography to test stability. ::: {#7e302e38 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} splits = make_splits(data) print_frame( "Split sizes", pd.DataFrame( { "rows": { "development train": len(splits.development_train), "development validation": len(splits.development_validation), "final train": len(splits.train), "untouched test": len(splits.test), }, "exposure": { "development train": splits.development_train["Exposure"].sum(), "development validation": splits.development_validation[ "Exposure" ].sum(), "final train": splits.train["Exposure"].sum(), "untouched test": splits.test["Exposure"].sum(), }, } ), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The three branches of each deviance are visible in the source below. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `weighted_mean_deviance` ::: {#743e5405 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(weighted_mean_deviance) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def weighted_mean_deviance( y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, weight: np.ndarray, component: str, tweedie_power: float, ) -> float: """Compute the component-appropriate weighted mean deviance.""" if component == "frequency": return float(mean_poisson_deviance(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=weight)) if component == "severity": return float(mean_gamma_deviance(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=weight)) return float( mean_tweedie_deviance( y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=weight, power=tweedie_power, ) ) ``` ::: ::: Three things to notice: - the **family** comes from `TARGET_SPECS` — Poisson for frequency, Gamma for severity, Tweedie-weighted deviance for pure premium; - the **weight** is the row-appropriate exposure or claim count, so a six-month policy really does count half as much as a twelve-month one; - the deviance is per-element (one observation of the response distribution), and `sklearn` averages them with the same weights the model used in fitting — that is what makes the fitted GLUM models' training deviances and deviances on the test set directly comparable. ::: ## Check portfolio-level calibration **Why:** a useful ranking can still charge too much or too little in total. Portfolio calibration asks whether total expected claims match total observed claims. **What we do:** calculate test actual/expected (A/E), observed total, and predicted total for frequency, severity, and pure premium. **Best practice:** A/E near 1 is necessary but not sufficient. Quantify its uncertainty and repeat by meaningful segments and time periods; a perfect portfolio A/E can hide offsetting errors between customer groups. ::: {#1eb00f4f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} for component, predictions in ( ("frequency", frequency_predictions), ("severity", severity_predictions), ("pure_premium", pure_premium_predictions), ): print_frame( f"{component.replace('_', ' ').title()} portfolio calibration", portfolio_calibration_table(splits.test, component, predictions), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Test ranking ability with Lorenz curves and Gini **Why:** pricing needs to order safer and riskier policies, not merely hit the portfolio mean. A monotonic rescaling can preserve ranking while changing A/E. **What we do:** order test policies from low to high predicted pure premium, then plot cumulative exposure against cumulative capped loss. The Gini coefficient summarized below is `1 − 2·AUC` of that curve. **Best practice:** higher positive Gini is better, but inspect the full curve. A lower curve dominates only when it does not cross; crossing curves are not a ranking victory. Ranking evidence never replaces calibration evidence. ### Build the Lorenz curve by hand For one prediction, the ordered Lorenz curve is the consistent pairing of the cumulative exposure share and the cumulative observed loss share after sorting policies low-to-high by predicted rate. Ties are averaged into a single block so the curve does not depend on the test-set row order. ::: {#0096778a .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} y_test = splits.test["PurePremium"].to_numpy(dtype=float) exposure = splits.test["Exposure"].to_numpy(dtype=float) ``` ::: ::: {#7e301013 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} reference = "LightGBM Tweedie" ref_pred = pure_premium_predictions[reference] sorted_df = ( pd.DataFrame({"y": y_test, "p": ref_pred, "w": exposure}) .sort_values("p") .assign(wy=lambda d: d["y"] * d["w"]) ) blocks = sorted_df.groupby("p", sort=False)[["w", "wy"]].sum() cum_exposure = np.r_[0.0, blocks["w"].cumsum()] cum_observed_x_exposure = np.r_[0.0, blocks["wy"].cumsum()] F = cum_exposure / cum_exposure[-1] L = cum_observed_x_exposure / cum_observed_x_exposure[-1] fig, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5)) axis.plot(F, L, label=f"{reference} (by hand)") axis.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls=":", color="grey", label="diagonal") axis.set_xlabel("Cumulative exposure share") axis.set_ylabel("Cumulative observed loss share") axis.set_title(f"Ordered Lorenz curve ({reference})") axis.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](pure_premium_tutorial_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=514 height=449} ::: ::: Good models bow the curve below the diagonal (loss concentrated in the last fraction of predicted exposure). The area under the diagonal is `1/2`, so the area *between* the diagonal and the curve is `1/2 − AUC`. ### Compute the Gini coefficient by hand There are three equivalent faces of the same definition: 1. **Mean-absolute-difference form** (Gini's original), `G = Σᵢ<ⱼ wᵢ wⱼ |yᵢ − yⱼ| / (W² μ)`. Conceptually clearest, O(n²). 2. **Area form** (the Census Bureau and most actuarial software), `G = 1 − 2·AUC` where the AUC is the area under the ordered Lorenz curve. `np.trapezoid` computes this *exactly* when the curve is piecewise-linear. 3. **Average-rank form** (the Frees–Meyers–Cummings convention adopted here), `G = 2·Σᵢ wᵢ yᵢ F̄ᵢ / Σᵢ wᵢ yᵢ − 1`, with midrank CDF `F̄ᵢ = (W_{i-1} + wᵢ/2) / W`. Closed form, O(n log n), and naturally tie-safe. All three are equal whenever predicted rates are distinct. With ties — common when a model only uses categorical risk factors — the *area* form depends on the within-tie row order (verified below: swapping two tied policies changes the value), whereas the *average-rank* form aggregates tied blocks into a single step and is permutation-invariant by construction. ::: {#43e22f4b .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} hand_F = (np.cumsum(blocks["w"]) - blocks["w"] / 2) / blocks["w"].sum() gy_by_hand = 2 * (blocks["wy"] * hand_F).sum() / blocks["wy"].sum() - 1 library_gini = gini(y_test, ref_pred, exposure) accuracy_row = evaluate_predictions( splits.test, "pure_premium", {reference: ref_pred}, selected_power ).loc[reference] print(f"By-hand Gini (midrank): {gy_by_hand:.6f}") print(f"Library gini(...) : {library_gini:.6f}") print(f"evaluate_predictions raw_gini: {accuracy_row['raw_gini']:.6f}") np.testing.assert_allclose(gy_by_hand, library_gini, atol=1e-12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` By-hand Gini (midrank): 0.322190 Library gini(...) : 0.322190 evaluate_predictions raw_gini: 0.322190 ``` ::: ::: The library and the by-hand value agree to machine precision; both equal the `raw_gini` column that `evaluate_predictions` already reports. ### Tie order-dependence, demonstrated The naive `np.trapezoid` over a stable-sorted array (the old implementation) **depends on the order of tied policies**, which is the row order of the test set. The midrank formula does not: ::: {#879a4a7b .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} def old_polygonal_gini(y, p, w): order = np.argsort(p, kind="stable") cw = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(w[order])] cl = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(w[order] * y[order])] return 1 - 2 * np.trapezoid(cl / cl[-1], cw / cw[-1]) y_demo = np.array([5.0, 1.0, 3.0]) p_demo = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 1.0]) w_demo = np.ones(3) print(f"old polygonal (given order): {old_polygonal_gini(y_demo, p_demo, w_demo):.4f}") print( "old polygonal (tied pair swapped): " f"{old_polygonal_gini(y_demo[::-1], p_demo[::-1], w_demo[::-1]):.4f}" ) print(f"midrank (given order): {gini(y_demo, p_demo, w_demo):.4f}") print( "midrank (tied pair swapped): " f"{gini(y_demo[::-1], p_demo[::-1], w_demo[::-1]):.4f}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` old polygonal (given order): 0.2963 old polygonal (tied pair swapped): 0.1481 midrank (given order): 0.2222 midrank (tied pair swapped): 0.2222 ``` ::: ::: For real data with tied predictions (e.g. a GLUM on categorical-only features) the two implementations can disagree by several points of Gini. Equal to the area form when there are no ties; differs from it once ties exist. - **Vendor grids (e.g. some Emblem-style prints)** use a cumulative-weight grid with unit-weight-adjusted constants (`(0.5·(shift+1)).cumsum() + (0.5·(w−1)).cumsum()`). On integer row weights all conventions agree, but on fractional exposures they differ in the third decimal. The midrank convention adopted here is exact on any positive weights. - **Unweighted forms** written as `ΣSᵢ / T − (n+1)/2` over data sorted descending by prediction return *half* the standard Gini (a factor of 2 is missing). That bug is hidden when the consumer divides it by itself, because every normalized Gini ratio cancels the scale error. Worth checking for in any textbook or package you reuse. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `lorenz_curve` and `gini` ::: {#1afd902f .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(lorenz_curve) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def lorenz_curve( y_true_rate: np.ndarray, y_pred_rate: np.ndarray, weight: np.ndarray, ) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """Return a low-to-high Lorenz curve including both endpoints. Tied predictions are aggregated into a single block so the curve is permutation-invariant. The block midpoint is reached once, giving a straight line across the tied block (the standard convention when average ranks are used). """ y_true_rate = np.asarray(y_true_rate, dtype=float) y_pred_rate = np.asarray(y_pred_rate, dtype=float) weight = np.asarray(weight, dtype=float) if np.any(weight <= 0) or weight.sum() <= 0: raise ValueError("Lorenz weights must be positive") order = np.argsort(y_pred_rate, kind="stable") sorted_pred = y_pred_rate[order] sorted_weight = weight[order] sorted_observed = y_true_rate[order] _, starts = np.unique(sorted_pred, return_index=True) block_weight = np.add.reduceat(sorted_weight, starts) block_observed = np.add.reduceat(sorted_weight * sorted_observed, starts) cumulative_weight = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(block_weight)] cumulative_loss = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(block_observed)] cumulative_weight /= cumulative_weight[-1] if cumulative_loss[-1] > 0: cumulative_loss /= cumulative_loss[-1] return cumulative_weight, cumulative_loss ``` ::: ::: The tied-prediction block is detected with `np.unique(return_index=True)` and reduced with `np.add.reduceat` on `sort=False` *or* ascending, so a straight line spans the block instead of wiggling through within-tie row order. The (0, 0) and (1, 1) endpoints come from the leading `0.0` in the cumulative arrays and the final normalization. ::: {#3fb9774b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(gini) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def gini( y_true_rate: np.ndarray, y_pred_rate: np.ndarray, weight: np.ndarray, ) -> float: """Compute the weighted Gini coefficient for a low-to-high ordering. Uses the average-rank (midrank) closed form G = 2 * sum_i (w_i y_i Fbar_i) / sum_i (w_i y_i) - 1, Fbar_i = (W_{i-1} + w_i / 2) / W, which is the Frees-Meyers-Cummings convention. Tied predictions are aggregated into single blocks so the value is permutation-invariant; the resulting Gini equals 1 - 2 * AUC of the tie-corrected polygonal Lorenz curve. Returns ``numpy.nan`` when total weighted loss is not positive (no average can be defined). """ y_true_rate = np.asarray(y_true_rate, dtype=float) y_pred_rate = np.asarray(y_pred_rate, dtype=float) weight = np.asarray(weight, dtype=float) if np.any(weight <= 0) or weight.sum() <= 0: raise ValueError("Gini weights must be positive") order = np.argsort(y_pred_rate, kind="stable") sorted_pred = y_pred_rate[order] sorted_weight = weight[order] sorted_observed = y_true_rate[order] _, starts = np.unique(sorted_pred, return_index=True) block_weight = np.add.reduceat(sorted_weight, starts) block_weighted_y = np.add.reduceat(sorted_weight * sorted_observed, starts) total_weight = block_weight.sum() total_loss = block_weighted_y.sum() if total_loss <= 0: return float("nan") cumulative_weight = np.cumsum(block_weight) f_mid = (cumulative_weight - block_weight / 2) / total_weight return float(2.0 * (block_weighted_y * f_mid).sum() / total_loss - 1.0) ``` ::: ::: The closed form is equivalent to `1 − 2·AUC` of the same polygonal curve, and avoids `np.trapezoid` entirely. Returning `numpy.nan` when the total weighted loss is not positive is a deliberate departure from the silent `if total > 0` guard the old version had — a degenerate response should not get a confidently wrong number. ::: ## Inspect single-model lift by predicted-risk decile **Why:** lift makes ranking concrete: it asks whether observed pure premium rises with the risk bands that a model predicts. **What we do:** divide test exposure, from safest to riskiest prediction, into ten equal-exposure bins and compare observed and predicted pure premium. **Best practice:** use equal exposure rather than equal policy counts when policies have different durations. Inspect credibility, uncertainty, and irregular deciles instead of choosing a model from one impressive endpoint. model_a_prediction: np.ndarray, model_b_prediction: np.ndarray, exposure: np.ndarray, n_bins: int = 10, ) -> pd.DataFrame: """Bin observed rates by the low-to-high model-A/model-B prediction ratio.""" y_true_rate = np.asarray(y_true_rate, dtype=float) model_a_prediction = np.asarray(model_a_prediction, dtype=float) model_b_prediction = np.asarray(model_b_prediction, dtype=float) exposure = np.asarray(exposure, dtype=float) if n_bins < 1: raise ValueError("n_bins must be at least 1") if not np.all(np.isfinite(exposure) & (exposure > 0)): raise ValueError("exposure must be finite and positive") if not np.all(np.isfinite(model_a_prediction) & (model_a_prediction > 0)): raise ValueError("model_a_prediction must be finite and positive") if not np.all(np.isfinite(model_b_prediction) & (model_b_prediction > 0)): raise ValueError("model_b_prediction must be finite and positive") ratio = model_a_prediction / model_b_prediction order = np.argsort(ratio, kind="stable") cumulative_exposure = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(exposure[order])] boundaries = np.linspace(0, cumulative_exposure[-1], n_bins + 1) bin_exposure = np.diff(boundaries) def rates(values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: cumulative = np.r_[0.0, np.cumsum(exposure[order] * values[order])] return ( np.diff(np.interp(boundaries, cumulative_exposure, cumulative)) / bin_exposure ) return pd.DataFrame( { "exposure": bin_exposure, "observed_rate": rates(y_true_rate), "model_a_rate": rates(model_a_prediction), "model_b_rate": rates(model_b_prediction), "prediction_ratio": rates(ratio), }, index=pd.RangeIndex(1, n_bins + 1, name="decile"), ) ``` ::: ::: The double-lift table is built the same way as the single-model lift table: policies are sorted by the model-A / model-B ratio, cumulative exposure and cumulative A-rate, B-rate, and observed rates are computed, and `np.interp` splits boundary rows so the deciles are exactly equal-exposure.
